questions.stem: A student argues that an indigent defendant who cannot afford a lawyer is not entitled to one, because the state never hired him. Explain why that is mistaken.

answer.exemplar: The state may not send a person to prison for a serious offence without providing the assistance of counsel, so poverty cannot decide who is tried with a lawyer and who is not. On the separate question of statements, once a person is in custody and is being questioned, the failure to warn of the right to silence and to counsel means the resulting statement cannot be used against him, so the cost of an unwarned interrogation is the loss of the confession itself.

questions.explanation: The state may not imprison someone for a serious offence without counsel, and a statement taken in custody without the warnings cannot be used. Poverty is not a defence.
questions.hint: Separate the right to a lawyer from the cost of a statement.

questions.stem: A student believes the Fourteenth Amendment simply restated the Bill of Rights for the states. Explain why that is mistaken.

answer.exemplar: The Fourteenth Amendment did not reproduce the Bill of Rights. It made the states answer for deprivation of life, liberty or property without due process, and the courts then used that guarantee to hold the states to the same protections of speech, search and self-incrimination that already applied to the federal government. questions.topic: Where the first rule of suppression stopped
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the rule against suppression reached the states so late
questions.stem: A student asks why the protection against government suppression of speech was one of the last to bind the states. Explain the reason.

answer.exemplar: The First Amendment was drafted as a restraint on the federal government, and for most of the country's history the courts treated it as doing nothing to the states, which continued to punish speech and press through their own laws. Only when the Fourteenth Amendment was ratified, with its promise that no state shall deprive any person of life, liberty or property without due process, could the federal courts reach a state law. The protection therefore stopped at the federal government for roughly a century and a half before a constitutional route to the states existed.

questions.topic: Where the first rule of suppression stopped
questions.learningObjective: Identify the route by which the protection reached the states

stimulus.body: From a dissenting opinion: 'The freedom of the press and of speech, though not among the ancient rights of the people, is among the most valued and most essential of the rights of the modern citizen. If the state may silence the voice of the people at will, the constitutional protection of the freedom of speech becomes a shadow, and the people are left with nothing but the memory of it.'

questions.stem: The dissent above argues about a protection that did not reach the states when the case was decided. What is the correction to that gap?

options.text: The protection bound the federal government only; the Fourteenth Amendment supplied the route to the states.
The protection already reached the states, and the dissent objects to the way states had applied it.
options.misconception: Believes the protection had already reached the states

options.text: The protection reached the states only for matters of criminal procedure, and not for speech.
options.misconception: Restricts the reach to a procedural category

options.text: The protection was never extended to the states at all, so the gap persists to this day.
options.misconception: Believes the states were never reached

questions.explanation: The protection bound the federal government only, and the Fourteenth Amendment later supplied the route to the states. That closed the gap the dissent describes.
questions.hint: Ask which government the protection first constrained.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A guarantee that reached the states without the rule
questions.learningObjective: State how the later amendment bound the states

stimulus.body: Extract from a later amendment's text: 'No person shall be held to answer for a capital, or otherwise infamous crime, unless tried before a jury of the people, and with the right to the assistance of counsel for his defence.' A note records the year and the number of states that ratified it.

questions.stem: The amendment quoted above was adopted to extend a protection to the states. Which reading of its effect is accurate?

options.text: It bound the states through its own guarantees, rather than by restating the earlier amendments.
It made the earlier amendments applicable to the states word for word as written.
options.misconception: Says the amendment reproduces the earlier ones verbatim

options.text: It applied only to the federal government, leaving the states free to proceed without jury and counsel.
options.misconception: Reverses which government the amendment binds

options.text: It extended the protections of the earlier amendments to private employers as well.
options.misconception: Extends the amendment to private actors

questions.explanation: The amendment bound the states through its own guarantees rather than by repeating the earlier amendments word for word. It did not reach private employers.
questions.hint: Ask whether the amendment copies or restates earlier text.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Custody, counsel, and what a statement costs
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the counsel guarantee from the statement rule
questions.stem: A table reports that in a year the state provided appointed counsel in 82 per cent of felony trials and that 14 per cent of convictions followed a confession taken without counsel present. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The two figures describe separate guarantees, since counsel at trial and the rules on statements are distinct.
The confession figure shows counsel was generally ignored, because 14 per cent is a large share.
options.misconception: Treats the two statistics as the same measure

options.text: The 82 per cent figure shows counsel was regularly refused, since most trials lacked counsel.
options.misconception: Misreads 82 per cent as a failure rate

options.text: The confession figure proves that every statement taken without counsel was involuntary.
options.misconception: Equates absence of counsel with involuntariness

questions.explanation: The figures describe separate guarantees, since the share of trials with counsel and the share of convictions resting on an uncounseled statement measure different things. They are not one rate.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the two percentages actually counts.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: How much of a state trial a federal court would review
questions.learningObjective: Compute the number of petitions reaching a hearing on the claim
questions.stem: A table sets out that in one year 900 federal habeas petitions were filed, of which 610 were dismissed because the state courts had already given a full and fair hearing and 240 were dismissed after the state remedies were exhausted without success. Stage one, state what the court examines; stage two, count the petitions that reached a hearing.

options.text: The court examines the fairness of the state proceeding, and 50 petitions reached a hearing on the claim.
The court examines the sufficiency of the evidence, and 50 petitions reached a hearing on the claim.
options.misconception: Describes review of the facts rather than the process

options.text: The court examines the fairness of the state proceeding, and 850 petitions reached a hearing on the claim.
options.misconception: Counts the dismissals as hearings

options.text: The court examines whether the sentence was correct, and 50 petitions reached a hearing on the claim.
options.misconception: Describes a sentencing review instead

questions.explanation: The court asks whether the state proceeding was fair, and subtracting the two groups of dismissals from 900 leaves 50 petitions that reached a hearing. The rest were disposed of.
questions.hint: Subtract both groups of dismissals from the total filed.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Being tried twice, and the co-defendant who confessed
questions.learningObjective: Correct the belief that one transaction always means one offence
questions.stem: A student believes two charges arising from one transaction are always the same offence for double jeopardy purposes. Which correction is accurate?

options.text: They are the same only if each needs an element the other does not, so one act can support separate charges.
They are always the same, because one transaction can produce only one punishment.
options.misconception: Rests on the single-act rule alone

options.text: They are never the same, because two punishments cannot be imposed for one act at all.
options.misconception: Reads the rule on multiple punishments as barring charges

options.text: The test is whether the two charges carry the same punishment, so equal penalties make them one.
options.misconception: Uses the punishment rather than the elements

questions.explanation: The offences are the same only if each requires proof of an element the other does not. Two charges from one transaction can still be separate offences.
questions.hint: Ask what each charge requires the jury to find.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Prison labour, the cost of confinement, and the reform experiment
questions.learningObjective: Compare the cost of one prisoner with the cost of schooling
questions.stem: A table compares the annual cost of confining one prisoner at 192 dollars with the annual cost of schooling one child at 24 dollars. How many children could be schooled for the cost of confining one prisoner for a year?

options.text: Exactly 8 children could be schooled for that amount.
About 192 children could be schooled for that amount.
options.misconception: Divides by the wrong rate

options.text: About 24 children could be schooled for that amount.
options.misconception: Reports the cost per child as the number of children

options.text: About 168 children could be schooled for that amount.
options.misconception: Subtracts the two rates instead of dividing

questions.explanation: Dividing 192 dollars by 24 dollars a child gives exactly eight children, which shows how little a year of confinement buys outside the prison wall. The comparison is stark.
questions.hint: Divide the cost of confinement by the cost per child.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a crime rate can and cannot measure
questions.learningObjective: Explain why police and survey figures differ
questions.stem: A student argues that because the police figures and the survey figures differ, the survey must be wrong. Explain why that conclusion is not justified.

answer.exemplar: The two measures count different things. The police figures count offences that were reported and recorded, while the survey counts what people say happened to them, most of which never reached the police at all, so the survey figure is the larger one by design. The difference is not an error in either source but the measure of the part of crime that the official record never sees, which is why a recorded rate cannot be read as the amount of crime committed.

questions.explanation: The two sources count different things, offences recorded and offences reported to a survey, so the gap measures the part of crime the official record never sees. Neither source is wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what each source is actually counting.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Discretion and the death sentence
questions.learningObjective: Correct the belief that wider discretion removed the arbitrariness
questions.stem: A student believes that giving judges wider discretion in capital cases removed the arbitrariness. Which entry states the correction accurately?

options.text: Arbitrariness was met by requiring stated aggravating findings weighed against mitigating evidence.
Arbitrariness was removed by widening the range of sentences available to the judge.
options.misconception: Credits wider discretion with removing arbitrariness

options.text: Arbitrariness was removed because juries, not judges, now decide whether to impose the penalty.
options.misconception: Misstates who imposes the sentence after the reform

options.text: Arbitrariness was removed because the number of death sentences fell sharply after the reform.
options.misconception: Treats a lower number of sentences as the cure

questions.explanation: Arbitrariness was addressed by requiring stated aggravating findings and a weighing of mitigating evidence. Widening the range of choice open to the judge was not the answer.
questions.hint: Ask what the reform required the sentencer to do.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A sentence fixed by quantity rather than by conduct
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the steps that fix a sentence under a quantity rule
questions.stem: A table traces the order in which a sentence is fixed where the penalty is set by quantity. Which order is correct?

options.text: The quantity seized is established, the range for it is identified, and the sentence is fixed within it.
The statutory range is identified, the quantity seized is established, and the sentence fixed within it.
options.misconception: Looks up the range before the fact that fixes it is known

options.text: The sentence is fixed within the range, the quantity seized is established, and the range is identified.
options.misconception: Fixes the sentence before establishing the quantity

options.text: The quantity seized is established, the sentence fixed within the range, and the range is identified.
options.misconception: Identifies the range after the sentence has been chosen

questions.explanation: The quantity is established first, the statutory range for that quantity is then identified, and only then is the sentence fixed within it. Each step depends on the last.
questions.hint: The fact that fixes the range must come first.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the evidence said about changing an offender
questions.learningObjective: State what a negative review does and does not establish

stimulus.body: From the review of programmes for offenders: 'We examined the studies available at the time and found no programme whose results could be demonstrated to reduce the rate of reoffending. We note, however, that most of the programmes examined were based on assumptions about the causes of offending that later work has challenged, and that a programme cannot be judged effective without a comparison group whose members receive nothing at all.'

questions.stem: The review above reaches a negative conclusion. Which statement best describes what the review itself allows the reader to conclude?

options.text: The programmes it examined had not been shown to work, which is a finding about those programmes alone.
No programme can reduce reoffending, because the review tested every programme in existence.
options.misconception: Generalises the finding to all programmes

options.text: Every programme of that period was tested and failed, so the design of the studies was sound.
options.misconception: Claims the review tested every programme

options.text: The review shows that the comparison group was the reason the programmes failed.
options.misconception: Misreads the note about comparison groups

questions.explanation: The review found only that the programmes it examined had not been shown to work. That is a finding about those programmes and not a proof about all of them.
questions.hint: Ask how far the review's finding can be carried.
